title: Fault-tolerant ripple-carry addition on Quantinuum Helios-1 with [[8,3,2]] + [[4,2,2]] error-detecting codes: 1-bit adder logical failure (6.0 +/- 5.9)e-5 vs (3.5 +/- 1.3)e-3 unencoded; 4-5-bit adders just above threshold
vendor: Quantinuum (Helios-1 hardware); experiment by an external team
organization: Quantinuum hardware; authors Nelson, Landahl, Baczewski
summary: Nelson, Landahl and Baczewski (arXiv:2610.14202, submitted 2026-10-09) run a universal fault-tolerant architecture built on two error-detecting codes, [[8,3,2]] and [[4,2,2]], on Helios-1. They compile ripple-carry adders for classical inputs up to five bits. An extra check that uncomputes a workspace qubit raises the effective fault distance of many circuit locations from two to four. After burst-error filtering, one-bit addition showed a single logical failure, an estimated logical failure rate of (6.0 +/- 5.9)e-5. Unencoded one-bit addition on the same hardware failed at (3.5 +/- 1.3)e-3. Two- and three-bit adders also improved over unencoded; four- and five-bit adders ran just above threshold.

key_specs.crossover: 1-3-bit adders below unencoded; 4-5-bit just above threshold

actionable: Encoded arithmetic beats unencoded on the project's anchor machine, but only at small sizes, and the headline rate rests on one failure event (about 98% relative uncertainty) with detection plus post-selection ('burst-error filtering'). It is not comparable to the knowledge base's logical-gate-error row, so no frontier change. For HYP-029-style budgets it only shows that distance-2 encoded arithmetic works below the unencoded rate at 1-3 bits.
notes: Numbers were checked against the arXiv abstract (export API, 2026-10-15). The abstract gives no physical error rate or threshold value despite the 'below-threshold' title. 'Threshold' appears to mean the encoded-versus-unencoded crossover (a pseudo-threshold); the full text was not read to confirm this.
